Get in touch Compute Sensing Future Compute Sensing Future The automotive industry is undergoing a fundamental transformation, shifting toward safe autonomous driving and enhanced in-cabin experiences.
This evolution places increasing demands on advanced automotive semiconductor technology.
And makes the automotive industry’s early engagement and alignment with the semiconductor roadmap essential for future mobility.

To support the automotive industry along this paradigm shift, imec develops advanced automotive chiplet integration, chiplet-based high-performance compute architectures, and next-generation automotive semiconductor technologies, enabling smarter, safer and more affordable mobility for everyone.
Interested in shaping the future of mobility?

Chiplet-based compute for automotive applications As advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS), autonomous capabilities, and immersive infotainment gain ground, the demand for computing power increases.

Through its autonomous edge chiplet program , formerly the automotive chiplet program, imec brings together a global, pre-competitive research consortium focused on defining, developing, and validating chiplet architectures for high-performance autonomous edge computing.
Supporting cost-effective and reliable automotive platforms.
Strengthening supply chain resilience across the semiconductor ecosystem.
As part of this effort, imec has also established the Advanced Chip Design Accelerator (ACDA) in Heilbronn, Germany, located at the Innovation Park Artificial Intelligence (IPAI).

Supported by the Ministry of Economic Affairs, Labor, and Tourism of Baden-Württemberg, ACDA expands imec’s chiplet research and validation capabilities through the development of automotive chiplet prototypes, multi-vendor integration and validation, and focused research on compute architectures tailored to automotive-grade requirements.

Imec offers a broad technology portfolio and support from research to manufacturing.

Non-terrestrial networks use satellites to extend mobile network coverage and enable connectivity between terrestrial users and networking infrastructure, including direct-to-cell (D2C) and direct-to-device (D2D) services.

Besides the massive infrastructural effort of putting large satellite constellations in orbit, NTN presents a number of challenges when it comes to payload electronics : Components must be extremely low-power and compact.
Even in low Earth orbit (LEO) or medium Earth orbit (MEO), radiation-tolerant or radiation-hardened electronics may be needed.
Imec has experience in space electronics and radiation-hardened IC design , with custom ASICs and sensors already operating in space.
Combining advanced research, system-level validation, and a route to custom-chip manufacturing within one organization, we're well-positioned to support your NTN electronics development.
Make sure to check out how we support semiconductor-driven ventures .
System and circuit RF IP for demanding NTN applications Imec's advanced system and circuit IP enables you to tackle requirements that cannot be met by off-the-shelf semiconductor IP.

Advanced RF materials and semiconductor processes 5G and 6G NTN require moving to higher frequencies and output-power levels , where conventional silicon CMOS or BiCMOS may not meet all efficiency and performance requirements, particularly in power amplifiers.
Imec's advanced RF research program investigates the material and process innovations needed to integrate III-V semiconductors with silicon CMOS in a cost-effective and scalable way.

RF interposer technology to enable the cost-effective integration of multiple semiconductor technologies (e.g., RF GaN or other III-V dies together with CMOS EIC dies) in a single package, with low loss even at high frequencies.
Optical connections are also playing a crucial role in high-performance compute and AI systems , for instance emerging concepts such as space-based computing and data-processing infrastructures.

Partner with us From digital intelligence to physical AI Artificial intelligence is entering a new era: bringing intelligence into the physical world with robots – changing every aspect of our lives.

Robotics evolves in stages, with successive generations of robots entering the market: Industrial and logistics robots performing repetitive, well-defined tasks in structured environments such as factories, warehouses and distribution centers, including assembly, inspection, material handling, picking, packing and autonomous mobile transportation.

Service robots operating alongside people in semi-structured environments such as hospitals, retail stores, airports, hotels and public spaces, supporting activities including inventory management, cleaning, delivery, security, healthcare assistance and customer interaction.

Advanced collaborative robots and autonomous assistants capable of understanding human intent, adapting to changing conditions and performing complex multi-step tasks in dynamic workplaces, construction sites, healthcare facilities and outdoor environments.

The intelligence embodied in future robots will rely on innovations across the entire technology stack , from advanced semiconductor technologies and ultra-low-power computing platforms to sensing, communications and AI.
Beyond technology innovation, imec acts as a neutral catalyst for the robotics ecosystem .

As no single player can master the full robotics value chain, successful innovation requires close collaboration between hardware suppliers, AI developers, system integrators and application partners.
Addressing the key challenges of autonomous robotics Deploying robots in the real world remains one of today's greatest technological challenges.
Full autonomy demands capabilities that must work flawlessly from day one: robust perception, real-time decision-making, safe operation, energy efficiency, reliability and data privacy.

AI-powered robots rely on increasingly sophisticated models to understand their surroundings, make decisions and execute actions, all this while minimizing latency and energy consumption, and maximizing safety and performance.
This will require computing architectures that span multiple levels, from ultra-efficient, ultra-low power on-device processing and edge AI to cloud-based computing resources.
Energy efficiency and endurance .

But we’re also working towards photovoltaic systems that can generate hydrogen from ambient moisture.

Iuliana Radu, program director for beyond CMOS and quantum computing at imec, discusses how these high-performance computers might look like in 2035.
Wearables and ingestibles will continuously monitor our health, and combine the data with our genetic imprint.
Add to this the large amount of data generated by emerging IoT applications such as the autonomous cars, the smart buildings and the smart cities.
For both cloud computing and supercomputing, we will need solutions that bring computing to a higher level of performance, and this at the lowest possible energy consumption.
This enables different applications ranging from ultralow-power in the IoT space, to mobile and to high-performance computing.
On the eve of quantum computing Some applications are too complex to be solved with classical computing paradigms.
Quantum computing can come to the rescue.
In a quantum computer, information is manipulated in a fundamentally different way than in a classical computer.
Quantum computers operate with qubits that can with a certain probability be zero and with a certain probability be one.
Add to this entanglement, which means that qubits talk with each other and act concertedly, and the number of states in a quantum registry increases like a power law with the number of qubits.
Quantum computing promises the ability to solve those big problems, too difficult to solve on a classical computer.
Quantum computing can go beyond the capabilities of classical computing, but it will not be the ‘holy grail’ for solving all issues.
